An ugly truth in all of this is that this is all the result of political instability caused by bad prior decisions. Specificly three. And they all feed off each other.

1. America's unquestioning alliance with Israel and constant Middle East meddling. It has created the "war of choice" Israel forced on us via Trump. This has destabilized energy markets, creating mass inflation and economic stagnation due to an energy crisis.

2. America and Europe's failure to foresee Putin as a continuation of the old Russian Empire. We wanted good relations with Russia after the Soviet dissolution. So much that we pretended it no longer posed a threat. And cut defense spending and gave Moscow the benefit of the doubt despite increasing signs that it planned to keep going the same course of confrontation with its neighbors and Europe. Defense budgets were cut. Deals with Russia were cut. America and Europe became dependent on the cheap energy markets its oil and gas provided. We let Putin get away with invading his neighbors and set a precedent by doing nothing.  And now we are caught flat-footed.

3. Inaction by the US in migrating off oil to renewables and other energy sources. China now has the technological and manufacturing lead in tomorrow's energy sources. Sources that are much less affected by geopolitical instability and geography. This is why China has basically been untouched by the current energy crisis.

My husband was diagnosed with MS in 2013, on the basis of a spinal lesion, optic neuritis and oligoclonal bands. Since then, he has (thankfully) had zero disease progression. However, he suffers from symptom flare-ups of his balance deriving from the spinal lesion. He also has bad side effects from his medication. 

We have wondered whether he was misdiagnosed. However, I'd be interested to know how doctors are certain of a misdiagnosis. It's a risky assessment to make because if someone is truly misdiagnosed, then they can safely stop taking MS treatment drugs. However, if doctors are wrong about the misdiagnosis, then stopping the treatment can cause a relapse. 

In any case, I think the bottom line here is that we still have a pretty poor understanding of these diseases.

I haven't given up, but have accepted that life is a mystery and we don't get neat solutions. I went to ER and was told I had a mini-stroke.  They immed put me on blood thinners and wanted to admit me.  I only had one of the symptoms; a frozen arm and fingers.  The other symptoms, drooping face, slurred vision dizziness and confusion, I didn't have.  I drove myself and declied to be admitted

I went to another well-respected hospital w/i 3 days and was able to see the head neurologist who said he doubted that I had a stroke.  My office visit with him (arm had ret'd to normal within 2 days), I passed all the standart tests like touching your nose with your finger w/eyes closed, grip test, push pull test.  Just to be sure he still ordered tests, which was fine  He immed. took me off the blood thinners.  I wore a heart monitor for 14 days and went several CT scans as well as cervical spine.  The only thing that turned  up was a bulging back disc (I'm mid 70's_) and I'm going to outpatient physical therapy for that now.

Of course I cancelled all the follow up visits at the initial place.  They would have sent me down chasing rabbit holes running up huge bills

what I turned out to have; what they call Saturday night palsy.  I fell asleep in a chair watching youtube (no I didn't pass out from drinking because I don't drink).  But my arm was pressed against the arm of the chair anad head tilted forward which caused the stop of blood flow.  Once lifted, it started again which reversed itself.

Always if you can get a second opinion.  I'm thankful it was no more than that.

comments.name: Rich
comments.body:
I think the author misses the biggest commonality between the Cornell case and the case she describes—namely, the use of alcohol and drugs by the victims. Alcohol is the oldest “date rape” drug known. Jane Doe was underage for drinking at the time of the assaults. By her own account, she drank heavily before even going to the frat house, including at her sorority and at a bar where she hid her underage hand markings. She then drank more at the frat house before agreeing to have sex with someone she knew and someone she didn’t, and was subsequently pressured into taking ketamine, and later sexually assaulted.

In the FIT case, one of the women asked a male acquaintance to bring them cocaine, and they took the offered drugs willingly. Tragically, they were given fentanyl instead; like all who use street drugs, they fell victim to the reality that you never truly know what you are getting.

In what world do these women not bear some responsibility for putting themselves in an exceptionally vulnerable situation? You can give people all the prevention training you want, but if they put themselves in situations where they lack the mental or physical capacity to use that training, they are far more likely to be targeted. Alcohol is involved in 50% to 75% of acquaintance and date rapes, with rates up to 75% to 90% in campus sexual assaults. Leaving this out of the discussion does a disservice to young people just starting to independently explore the world.

comments.body:
I am impressed that Professor Senn has developed a very well thought out and comprehensive curriculum addressing the issue; I am hoping that it will ultimately have wide spread availability.

I also wonder is she or someone else could develop a comparable set of protocols for men. I think such a program would be even more vital for men, who are almost  invariably the instigator of sexual abuse.  Women would still need to be attentive to their safety, but perhaps the number of such incidents would decrease. Why do women have to bear responsibility for preventing sexual attacks? The burden should be on those that infringe on the safety of women.

Others have commented that not all men should be blamed, and of course that is true.  But it is hard to know which men are capable of such behavior. It only takes one man to irreparably impact a woman's life forever.

comments.name: Johan Pablo
comments.body:
I wonder about several factors at play here: expanding notions of what we consider assault, the narrative of vulnerability and victimhood that we foist upon young women, the wariness of young men we instill in them, and social media's tendency to demand conformity and amplification. My suspicion is that the tragic story about the FIT student hasn't gained as much traction for the very reason that it is just that, a horrific story we wish had never happened, and not a cultural-political Rorschach test full of ambiguity and problematizing evidence. I suspect Times writers and editors understand this on some level, hence the Cornell case continuing to make rounds weeks after airing in the headlines, despite the veneer of narrative cohesion between staff writers. 

Over the past couple years, the meme question for young women, "Would you rather encounter a bear or a man while hiking alone in the woods?" has highlighted the extent to which women see implicit threats in men (women, seemingly overwhelmingly, choose the bear). At a certain point, I too suspect that such fear must be more limiting and protective. It cannot be helpful for young heterosexuals who aspire to date their peers, let alone get married and form families. 

From where I stand, getting hurt, badly, appears intrinsic to the human condition. We should work to mitigate it where possible but not let ourselves be consumed by it.

Having fun and enjoying your college years is one thing; deliberately giving up your control and self awareness is another! I’m not “blaming the victim” but young women should use their common sense.

comments.body: I appreciate this reporting and recollections of Jeff Schmaltz and other gay men at the NYT. It certainly did take tremendous courage in those days, in the 1980s and early 1990s, to be public about living with HIV. Jeff followed in the footsteps of the earliest gay men with the virus who in 1983 declared in the document known as the “Denver Principles” that they should be known as “people with AIDS.”  Not AIDS victims or even patients. They wanted to be identified foremost by their humanity, not by a stigmatizing medical diagnosis. Those men were my role models as well when I received surprising news in October 2005. After reporting in Washington DC on HIV-AIDS as an HIV-negative gay man, I suddenly had to figure out how to tell my story. Like Jeff and those earliest men, I chose to tell it as a heroic journey toward finding my own resilience and strength. I am far more fortunate than my role models in that I am the beneficiary of highly effective treatment that did not exist in their time. Thank you for remembering and reminding us of Jeff.

comments.name: JAMES GOODLETT
comments.body:
What drives me crazy is that the WSJ puts conjecture to the fold without finalizing details for the reader!

1. Actual Debt Exposure Remains Unknown: The article estimates billions in potential borrowing capacity but never establishes how much Ellison actually owes across the five banks or his total debt relative to liquid assets.

2. Loan Costs and Terms Are Missing: Without disclosing interest rates, repayment schedules, collateral requirements, and lending covenants, the article cannot accurately assess the true financial cost or sustainability of Ellison's borrowing strategy.

3. Significant Risk of Margin Calls: The article fails to examine how a substantial decline in Oracle, Tesla, or other pledged stock valuations could trigger margin calls, forced asset sales, and potentially broader market consequences.

4. Corporate Governance and Conflicts of Interest: Although Oracle's board reportedly reviews Ellison's borrowing arrangements quarterly, the article does not adequately investigate potential conflicts between his personal financial obligations, corporate decision-making, and shareholder interests.

5. Incomplete Analysis of Tax Avoidance: The article highlights the "buy, borrow, and die" strategy without quantifying Ellison's potential capital-gains tax savings or explaining how borrowing costs, estate taxes, and stepped-up cost basis ultimately affect the strategy's financial benefits.

This is a vey important, stunningly apt piece of writing. Only in the last few decades two to six, I'd say, have we found the knowledge the human genome has to offer, 

I don't have an auto immune diseas, as far as I know. But I do have an ALLO immune disease, because a chunk of the genome in my body, I don' know how much except orobably all of my bone marrow, came from someone else. I don't know who, but I believe he is a German, late 20's or so, and quite possibly present or former military.

I also know thst his immune system and mine were as near a perfect match as the gigantic databases here, in Germany, and elsewhere, could find. Had they not been found, I would have died of acute myeloid leukemia about seven years ago. 

But I'm alive. No AM, and it will not be likely not return say the geniuses, really,of medicine--no kidding--who cured me. You won't hear that word in Provider Land very often. But that's what happened.

First they killed my own marrow which was killing me. Not fun. Then they fave me new, clean blood --made by his marrow which I retain today.

However, the T cells on the lookout for disease in my donor's genome now attack me. My tear glands are gone, I get rashes sometimes. I have some lung issues. But I just power-walked two miles uophill, and I feel great. Immuno suppressive help. I have a chance to be opmpletely well someday. But I'm not waiting. I write music and sing and I wrote a song about my experience called, with large irony: Too White.

The notion that an autoimmune response is a "hypervigilant" immune response is a simplification of matters, as immune response is incredibly varied and a big factor is "immune tolerance" induction via the thymus.

comments.name: Jesse
comments.body: I have four autoimmune diseases: MS; PBC; NAFLD; Sjogren's.  I also have two incurable lung diseases: Bronchiectasis and Cryptogenic Organizing Pneumonia (caused by an antibiotic and misdiagnosed for four months as I kept taking the antibiotic and the COP worsened). No history of autoimmune disease in my families and we can go back centuries. I wish I knew what caused them because they ruined my life and work. I went on disability November 2004 and have never gone back as I was diagnosed with one disease after another. But my MS is interesting: no new lesions since diagnosis in March 2006; 8 years for complete rehabilitation (I had to learn to walk a second time as an adult); I have full cognitive and memory functions (I am bilingual and taught grad courses in Paris); I could never take the frontline treatments for MS, the first almost killed me (admitted with a heart rate of 34) and the doctors said no more attempts at treatment with, say, Tysabri; I jokingly asked my neuro if there were any "organic" meds for MS.  We finally came up with ivIG and Solumedrol, the latter I had been taking for a year in 3-day and 5-day treatments, 500mg a day. I'm down to 125mg for two-day treatments with ivIG, every 3 weeks.  It's the PBC that is the problem. I've had it for about 30 years, I'm 6 years into cirrhosis according to CT scans, but the blood tests haven't caught up with the scans. (ALT and AST are normal.)  They ruined my life; but I'm still alive for what it's worth.

Cell service and home Wi-Fi is another $300 per month. They put a little each month toward life insurance, their children’s college accounts and retirement."

Discussions about medication-induced insomnia often fall into a basic pharmacological trap: treating sleeplessness as a simple side effect of individual drugs. As a doctor, I have come to realize that insomnia is rarely a binary switch tripped by a single drug but a physiological perturbation acting on a fundamentally altered baseline. Sleep is an active process requiring initiation—via GABAergic and adenosine gating—and maintenance withexcitatory monoaminergic drive. As we age, nervous system inherently vulnerable to hyperarousal.
Layered onto this baseline is a profound environmental mismatch. Since electric lighting, and now evening blue light from screens, retinal cells constantly signal the suprachiasmatic nucleus to suppress nocturnal melatonin. Further modern dietary factors—such as metabolic excitation from processed foods that suppress GABA receptors while heightening dopaminergic tone—create a persistent state of hyperarousal that contrasts sharply with calming botanical modulators like turmeric. Circadian lifestyle changes have rendered insomnia almost inevitable.
Against this noisy background, drugs modulate central nervous system tone. Lipophilic beta-blockers readily cross the blood-brain barrier to disrupt noradrenergic signaling and suppress pineal melatonin, whereas hydrophilic counterparts spare central sleep architecture. Generic actions of common medications produce vastly different clinical responses depending on this underlying neurochemical balance.

How many articles does Wikipedia feature? A gazillion? It seems that trying to characterize Wikipedia in all its multiplicity is like trying to sum up a jungle. Or an ocean. Sure, there's some articles or parts of articles that bite or slither, but how much of it is just plain useful, informative, fascinating?

Why shouldn't one trust Mr. Wales, Wikipedia's aspiration of transparency and the organization's non-profit structure more than the weird musings & obsessions and suspect motivations of the opaque edgelord Elon Musk, whose Right Wing Political Correctness (repackaged as his own form of Wokeism) is performative, instrumental and opportunistic?

To each his own, I guess. We live in an age of deep skepticism. We've lost faith in our powers of discrimination. If it's not all true, nothing is true. The cultural moment is a kind nihilism lite. It, too, will pass . . . but God knows whether we recalibrate to a new low or whether we rebound and recover.

The free ranging animal spirits of today's extremisms cannot help but view Wikipedia suspiciously. Today it's fashionable to trust a weirdo more than a professor. No man is more earnest than a purveyor of unpasteurized milk or Ivermectin or bleach. And so we have Grokipedia instead of Wikipedia. I mean, after all, who would you rather trust: the volunteers who shepherd Wikipedia, who curate it & tend to it for free or anonymous minions and money grubbing, machine-scraping opacity of Elon's alternative?

I have often been frustrated by the discordant, chopped-up nature of articles, primarily historical ones, that I researched on Wikipedia. Nevertheless, it was valuable, and aside from a trip to a major library, there was no viable alternative.  Now I use AI apps, delicately and discreetly, to fill the gaps in Wikipedia. 

I recently traced the provenance of a pistol from a factory in the US, to a component of US war-aid provided  to Chiang Kai-shek's KMT, to its probable capture by Communist forces, to the Red Army's likely use of it when they entered the Korean War in 1950, to a US soldier (a friend) who served in that war and took it home to the US as a war trophy.  This was not presented as provenance-proven, iron-clad history but as a combination of possibilities and likelihoods.  Neither Wikipedia nor, so much less, Britannica could have provided this detailed surmise.

Different sources provide different values.  I still use Britannica, Wikipedia, and AI, each of which is subject to errors, prejudice, or unwitting distortions. As a researcher, the important thing is to be open-minded but alert and wary.  True for citizens as well.

Gemini, being able to quickly access and organize a huge amount of information,  and misinformation,  often provides responses that are aimed directly at my query.  However, the extent to which it is encyclopedic is impossible to know,  a propietary "black box".  I have learned to request specific information sources,  but it delivers a response, regardless, that  provides  high praise to the insight in my query  (I am apparently an undiscovered genius, at age 78).  When it is wrong, it is often because it using old information to respond to a query about a something that is changing rapidly.  As is so often the case with products of for-profit massive corporations whose only legal responsibility is to  shareholders to maximize profit,  I am wary (from experience) that its power, at times, is being used to provide a response  that is personalized to taste sweet,  but is sometimes sweet poison.  A Wikipedia entry is written with no knowledge of me,  and most of the time,  to survive,  has to state the facts pretty much as they are known.    I would recommend great care in mixing AI into Wikipedia.

These articles are always useful to the lay person who is new to this sort of advice. But I find it frustrating that at this point we are still just talking about diet, exercise, sleep, no smoking, less alcohol and more social connections. Yes, these are very important, but there are new things to talk about. Vaccines such as HSV have been shown to decrease the incidence of dementia (not to mention shingles). If your cholesterol is high, consider adding Ezetimibe to your cholesterol lowering regimen. Recent research has found up to an 85% reduction in dementia risk. GLP-1s may not just lower weight, they may have cognitive benefits and anti-inflammatory benefits as well. Much research still needs to be done, but at this point an overweight person should not be asking whether they should start a GLP-1 but rather is there any reason for them not to? High Vitamin D levels are linked to better cognitive performance in individuals with double APOE4 and thus a recommendation for Vit D supplementation (which has few downsides) is reasonable. Drinking 2-3 cups of filtered (paper filter only) caffeinated coffee a day is linked to lower risk of dementia even in APOE4 patients.
Including this type of information in a future article (which could also talk about all the standard topics) would make it much more interesting to a wide range of readers.

For people, such as myself I am glad I've done some reading and understand that the article barely touches the surface of the emerging understanding of cognitive disorder.  At least the article might suggest further reading and discuss current research on issues such as triggers for inflammatory changes in the brain like use of alcohol or emerging studies on use if certain nutritional supplements such as Omega 3 Fatty Acids.  Not because these are proven cures but because there are studies to suggest benefit and might provide some added hope for individuals suffering with early cognitive problems or provide them with avenues to discuss more fully with their healthcare provider.  As a family physician I feel arming individuals with as much knowledge as possible and encouraging questions is an important part of information sharing.  And considering the probable multiple etiologies of cognitive disorder including but not limited to genetic risk I am not sure the title should seem to limit encouraging exercise to only those with genetic risk.

For years, South Carolina officials considered Rabies incidental, and made little effort to control or stop it.  Now, over half of the counties are reporting  confirmed cases of the disease.   Opportunistic and Infected fox, coyotes, skunks, and raccoons  now roam subdivisions that once were open or wooded land.  And, they stay in the area longer because of warmer winters.  To make matters worse, people are not getting their animals vaccinated against Rabies. 

This is an example of what happens  when you don't take a disease seriously.  Unfortunately, with state and federal cuts in fundings, I don't believe our state will ever "catch up."

Great article, thank you! 
The increase in reported cases is something to take note of.  However, we need to be careful no to over-blow the risk as it is still a very rare animal that is a carrier, except where localized outbreaks occur.  I worked with bats for 25+ years and worry about hysteria, which in the past resulted in large extermination efforts.  Research has show about 5% of bats infected, 10% of submitted raccoons, 19% of submitted foxes, and 20% of submitted skunks returned positive rabies tests. (CDC data from 2023, the last year reported).

RE Eric J and 16 shots required post-exposure to a rabid racoon; I'm really surprised it is that many shots. I know someone who had 3 shots post-exposure to a possibly rabies infected animal. The animal was never tested.

READ AT YOUR OWN RISK.

Huge Turturro fane here.

Turturro's performance in Robert Redford's 1994 historical drama, "Quiz Show" is masterful. He captures the angst and indignity of Herb Stempel, the long-reigning champion of the hit 1950s TV show, "Twenty-One". As his popularity begins to wane and ratings decline, the network decides to kick Stempel to the curb by fixing the outcome of the show with Stempel "throwing" a question that would have been a shoo in. Replaced by the suave, handsome, cultured Charles Van Doren, played superbly by the suave, handsome, cultured Ralph Fiennes, Stempel, a schlubby Queens homie becomes enraged. Turturro takes Stemple from disappointment to grief to resentment to anger and finally, to revenge. As part of a stellar ensemble cast including Rob Morrow, Paul Scofield and the aforementioned Ralph Fiennes, Turturro more than holds his own.  

By the way, Turturro fans who may have missed it might be interested in a quirky little film, "Fading Gigolo" a 2013 indie written, directed, and starring John Turturro, Liev Schreiber, and Woody Allen. Not great but entertaining. 

As to "The Only Living Pickpocket", I will see it of course, if for no other reason than Turturro's performance. Robert Bresson's 1959 French crime drama, "Pickpocket" explores the psychological aspects of a petty criminal operating in a big city.  Sounds like the Bresson film would be a great companion piece to "The Only Living Pickpocket".

I have advanced aphakic glaucoma and take 5 drops at night/4 in morning. I would loose my vision without them.

This happens for many reasons: phobias, pain, mobility, forgetfulness, cost of medication... the most worrying issue, however, is misperception regarding the importance of the medication. This happens most often when doctors do not *effectively* convey the necessity to comply.

As someone who has been on Spravoto (the FDA approved version of nasal ketamine) weekly, I have been through many situations in sessions, and many are unpredictable.   I would NOT be feel safe doing a treatment outside of a professional setting, even if this still included the pre-session check in.

I have had very strong reactions where I had no idea I was screaming, hysterically crying and more.  These are valuable reactions to bring forward in talk therapy,  but it is akso extremely important that there is someone to help talk me down while this is going on.  If I don't know I am screaming, how do I talk myself down?  If I am hysterically crying, again having a safety net of someone helping is key.

The importance of the routine of getting ready for a treatment, the trust that I have as a result makes for a far more effective session.  This is a key element as shown when so much talk therapy switched to telemedicine during Covid and one was not in the " safety" of a therapist's office.  There is no longer that luxury of being in a therapist's office but I personally have routines I follow to keep therapy at home somewhat containered.

I will also be one of the first people to say there was not always "safety" in a therapist's office.  The risk of ketamine treatments outside of a professional setting is far greater then the risk of what can happen by a lack of professionalism.

There is far more to be gained by focusing more new PTSD treatments then  at home ketamine

The attendant then left me but I was on camera and to wave my hand if I needed anything or push a call button.  She would come back after 40 minutes to check my blood pressure. Tears began pouring out my eyes and I felt like I was going to need to be revived.  Because I couldn’t move, none of the options given to me could I use. If you’re thinking about using this product be sure the clinic has a process to be physically with you while you are being treated.

This happens because over half of the population is over the age of 31, which means that their eyes are older than young children, so it is easier for them to believe and fall for the A.I. generated content. comments.name: Jonah S.
comments.body: From personal experience, I have never fallen for an AI video for more than a second. AI has a way of generating things, and it does that by making everything looking extremely good, an AI sounding voice, or both. After looking for half a second or listening for half a second, you can almost always tell that it’s AI. I personally believe that part of that is because I have experienced AI from the internet, and even other people showing it to me, that after time, it was easy to tell what has been generated by AI. I can understand if someone older, or very young would fall for AI, but I think anyone between the ages of 10 and 65 wouldn’t fall for an AI video. However, I have noticed an increase in quality from AI recently. If I were to look at an AI generated image or video 1-2 years ago, I would’ve instantly said it was AI. On the other hand, now I have to look for half a second or a second to tell if something is AI. The one thing that hasn’t changed is the voice. However, over time I personally think AI will become much more believable and realistic. At the current time though, I don’t experience thinking something is AI. There has been a single time I remember that it took me to finish the whole video to realise it was AI. The exception is that it was late at night, and very dark, whilst I was also outside. But even with that, it only took me 20-30 seconds to realise the video was fake. I genuinely think AI will become much more realistic, but right now, there's no problem.

comments.name: Corinne Gazda
comments.body: I think that my generation is very good at detecting AI because we have grown up with it. We do not blindly follow everything we see, and we can notice the small details. Parents always say that we spend too much time on our phones. In this case, I believe that works in our favor. Much like an AI database that can notice patterns and learn, we notice the patterns that AI generated images have, such as one too many fingers or that familiar sheen on the people’s skin. Other generations do not spend as much time on their phones, especially when they were young. People my age are more skeptical about what we see as well. Since we have grown up with AI, we have grown up knowing that not everything we see is real. In contrast, many older generations have been taught that things from a “reliable source” (such as the Santa Ana Police) are reliable. If I see something obviously unreal or even likely real, I do not automatically trust it. Because my generation has been learning about AI and how to spot it for so long, we are good at detecting it and understanding what it can do .

I might slightly doubt it because that kind of snake wouldn't belong here and that they wouldn't be very hard to find with its large body and the constant fear of people seeing it. It took me ten seconds of reverse-image search to find the same image, AI-generated, originally posted about a flood in another country an year ago. What struck me about the Southern California snake story is that the police fell for it first, an official warning was issued before anyone checked if the snake existed. That's what changed how I think about verification: "official source" no longer means "fact-checked." My rule now is to search the image myself before forwarding anything to family groups, because once my uncle shares something, thirty relatives believe it. The scariest part of AI isn't that fake photos exist. It's that "my dad sent it" still counts as evidence for most people I know.

Why do so many initiatives Beijing puts forward have “world” or “global” in their names:  World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization, the Global Civilization Initiative, the Global Development Initiative, and the Global Security Initiative. Beijing presents them as universally inclusive, but their emphasis is on cultivating non-Western partners, especially in the Global South, as a means of expanding Chinese influence and challenging Western leadership.

US restrictions on advanced chips and efforts to prevent unauthorized distillation create obstacles for Chinese AI developers. Chinese companies are also competing through widespread adoption, making many models available as downloadable open weights and offering low-cost services. Even without consistently leading at the frontier, they can build substantial influence by encouraging developers and businesses worldwide to build on their models.

This resembles aspects of China’s broader industrial strategy: use competitive pricing, scale, and state support to expand market share and make Chinese suppliers difficult to replace. Government subsidies have supported China’s EV expansion, while its dominance in critical-mineral processing and refining has created dependencies that Beijing exploits through export restrictions. My concern is that widespread adoption of Chinese AI could create another source of technological dependence and geopolitical leverage.

comments.name: R Mabry

Various controls on AI in China began months ago. 

Foreigners living and working in China are required to register their phones using their passports. Once that is done--and it is the law-- the access and use of Chinese AI apps are restricted (some are blocked, some require registration with a monthly fee but paying it does not necessarily guarantee access). Foreign apps such as ChatGPT are not accessible without a VPN, and since the latter is increasingly monitored, that option is a risky one. 

Unfortunately, some foreign visitors to China have insisted that they are able to access AI apps, but that is because they are using a non-China SIM card and are unregistered with Chinese government agencies. As with other matters, they return to their home country and sing praises of China without knowing that the day-to-day reality on the ground is more complicated and almost always, quite different from their own limited experience. 

There is a good deal to like about AI models originating in China. At the same time, it's yet another example of the dividing line between Chinese living in China (or overseas) and foreigners residing in China.

Truth is not always the only moral consideration. There are those who argue that a person may alter the truth for the sake of peace.
There is a difference between sparing someone needless pain and deceiving someone for personal gain, avoiding responsibility, or concealing wrongdoing.
The essential question is not simply whether our words are true or false, but why we might depart from the truth. Is it for sake of compassion, prevent harm, or preserve peace—or to serve our own interests?
Honesty without sensitivity can become cruelty, while compassion without honesty can become deception. The challenge is to honor both, recognizing that exceptions must serve a higher moral purpose, not merely personal convenience.

Tropical cyclones are a good example of how climate change can affect weather. 

Tropical cyclones derive their strength from warm water and much of the resulting damage is due to storm surge. Add heat to the system and a higher base sea level and you get more destructive storms.

I don’t think one can say that global warming caused Hurricane Sandy, but ocean temperatures were several degrees above normal for both Sandy and typhoon Haiyan and sea levels were higher than before the Industrial Revolution, so global warming exacerbated the storms. 

The extra foot or so of sea level rise on the US Northeast Coast caused Hurricane Sandy to flood an additional 25 square miles. (one foot of sea level rise, averaged globally moves the shoreline inland 300 feet, it’s worse in places like S Florida and Bangladesh).

Another interesting thing about Sandy. Changes in the northern polar jet stream, likely due to summer Arctic sea ice decline, allowed Sandy to follow an unusual, and unusually damaging course; directly into land with the dangerous semi-circle of the storm piling water ashore.

As if that weren’t enough, the translation speed of storm systems is slowing down and storms are holding more moisture so we’re seeing unusually large amounts of rain in storms like Harvey in Houston and Florence in the Carolinas.

Rapid intensification is becoming more of a problem as well giving people less time to evacuate.
